reason: Epicalyx segments have an acute or acuminate apex. The examples read as apex shape, but sharpness is a fair attribute for it. A rule could map acute/acuminate to the apex shape terms instead.
Trichomes can be nodose (knobbly, with swollen nodes). The examples are correct.
A perispore can be rugate (wrinkled or ridged). The examples are correct. Some of them describe the projections rather than the perispore.
Rachises and petioles are often flattened. The examples are correct.

'Cut' covers incised, -sect and lobed readings. The bearer is a leaf-type part, so the pair fits. The examples mix margin incision with whole-blade division (tripinnatisect). A rule would need to separate margin incision from blade dissection.
Wrong reading. 'Ligulate' here refers to the ligule at the sheath mouth, which is a separate part. 'Ribbonlike' alone is a weak basis. A leaf sheath is not strap-shaped.
A floral disc, or its glands, can be roughly square. The examples are correct.
Lithocysts or cystoliths can be punctiform (dot-like). The examples are correct.
Plant cells have a size, and the examples compare cells or give a size in µm.
Fruit valves have a length. The examples are correct, including the 'valves 7-10 x 10-12 mm' dimension pairs.
Rhizomes and their internodes can be solid rather than hollow. The examples are correct.
The examples say ellipsoid, which is not prolate in the strict sense. Prolate is only one kind of ellipsoid. A rule would need to map ellipsoid to the ellipsoid term, not to prolate.
A caruncle can be sessile (attached without a stalk). The examples are correct.
The examples are about the ribs of the sheath being conspicuous. The quality belongs to the ribs, not to the sheath. 'Conspicuous' is also too vague to be a useful value.
Secondary veins can be oblique to the midvein. The examples are correct.
A leaf sinus has a length or depth, often given as a fraction of the blade. The examples are correct.
An endocarp can be blotched, as in the examples.
Paraphyses can be orbicular (or suborbicular) in outline. The examples are correct.
A corolla tube can be dilated or expanded at the apex. The examples are correct.

A stem can be widened at the base. Some examples are plain width measures ('4.4-6.6 mm wide'). Others describe a branching angle ('wide'), which is a wrong reading, or cells that are 'not widened'. A rule would need to keep the widening reading and drop the angle and cell cases.
A corolla tube can be stout or thickened, including the thickened wall at the throat. The examples are correct.
The sporangium base (apophysis) has a colour. The examples are correct.
Axillary hairs can be inconspicuous. The examples are correct.
Axillary hairs in ferns are hyaline, but in the examples 'hyaline' mostly describes the distal cells. A rule would need to tell whether 'hyaline' applies to the hair or to its cells.
Wrong reading. 'Septate' means divided by cross-walls, not split. Hyaline cells being septate is also not a quality of the cell as a whole.
A pistillate flower has a position, such as axillary. The examples are correct.
A lemma can be rough, papillose or tuberculate. 'Pubescent' in one example is a different quality, which a rule could separate. The rest are correct.
A leaflet can be lunate (crescent-shaped). The examples are correct.

The examples describe pitchers, which are modified leaves in Nepenthes. Funnel-shaped fits them. A generic vascular leaf is not funnel-shaped, so the pair needs a pitcher bearer or a rule on pitcher words.
A moss peristome can be toothed or dentate. The examples are correct.
Bark has a colour. The examples are correct.
A domatium can be glabrous or hairy, so pilosity is a fair attribute. The examples are correct.
Perianth lobes can be reflexed. The examples are correct.

'Not bulbiferous' says that the plant bears bulbils. It does not say that the aerial tuber is present. The pair mixes up the part with what bears it. 'Aerial tubers absent' is a presence statement for another pattern.
A leaf lamina can carry cross bands (cross-zoned, banded). The examples are correct.
A leaf tooth has a height. The examples are correct.

The examples are a mix. The cypsela margin or beak can be straight or undulate, but 'beaks 3-10 mm' is a length and 'margins with ribs' is a different quality. A rule would need to keep only shape words.
Involucral bracts (phyllaries) can be translucent. The examples are correct. Some of them describe the midvein or the colour (tawny-transparent).
A peduncle or scape can be solid rather than hollow. The examples are correct.
A tuber can be vertical. The examples are correct.
A disk flower can be fertile or sterile. The examples are correct.
Involucral bracts can be narrow. The examples are correct.
The width in the examples is that of bark plates or flakes, not of the bark. A rule would need to say that this is the width of a plate, so the bearer would be the plate.
A corona lobe can be tubular. The examples are correct.
The bearer is the floral corona, and the examples are about an apex or a rounded back. The part may be a corona lobe or scale. A rule would need to say which part has the obtuse apex.
A leaf sheath clasps the stem, which is the usual sense of the word. The examples are correct.
A moss operculum has a height. The examples are correct.

'Characteristic' is a generic parent term. The examples are real root qualities (woody, fleshy, simple, branched) that belong to their own terms. A rule would need to assign them to specific values instead.
A peduncle can be reflexed or deflexed. 'Not strongly reflexed' is a negation, which a rule handles.
A gland (secretory tissue) can be lunate or crescent-shaped. The examples are correct.
A spike can be pendent. The examples are correct.
A perigynium wall has a thickness, as in the examples.
A leaf sheath can be firm (textured). The examples are correct.

'Characteristic' is a generic parent term. The examples are real bark qualities (fissured, ridged, smooth), but 'pruinose or glaucous' and 'peeled wood smooth' describe other parts. A rule would need to assign these to specific values.

This counts epicalyx segments or bractlets. The count is a valid quality of the epicalyx segment, and the examples are correct. The counted-parts rule may cover it, so check config/flora_counted_parts.tsv.
A rachilla (a higher-order inflorescence axis) can be stiff or rigid. The examples are correct.
The examples give a cleft or sinus depth between lobes, not the depth of the petal. A rule would need to attach it to the sinus or cleft, or to the petal lobing.
Wrong part. The examples are an apex or a spur (subglobose), which belong to another part. A short shoot is not described as subglobose in them.
Bracteoles can be strap-shaped or ligulate. The examples are correct.
A peduncle can be woody (ligneous). The examples are correct.
